clinicalPearls: Chorioamnionitis is inflammation or infection of the fetal membranes and amniotic fluid, most often from ascending organisms from the lower genital tract
It is strongly associated with prolonged rupture of membranes, prolonged labour, repeated vaginal examinations, and preterm labour
Clinical diagnosis is suggested by maternal fever combined with features such as maternal or fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, and purulent or foul-smelling amniotic fluid
Infection is typically polymicrobial, involving genital tract flora including anaerobes, group B streptococcus, and enteric organisms
Management centres on prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics and expediting delivery, as the infection will not resolve while the pregnancy continues
It is an important cause of maternal sepsis and can lead to postpartum endometritis, wound infection, and, rarely, septic shock
For the neonate it raises the risk of early-onset sepsis, pneumonia, and, particularly in preterm infants, neurological injury and cerebral palsy
Delivery does not preclude ongoing infection, so mother and baby require continued observation and treatment after birth
reference.pathophysiology: Chorioamnionitis most commonly results from ascent of bacteria from the vagina and cervix into the normally sterile amniotic cavity, particularly once the membranes are ruptured or the cervix is dilated. The organisms provoke a maternal and fetal inflammatory response with release of cytokines and prostaglandins that can precipitate or accelerate labour. Inflammation of the membranes, cord, and placenta may compromise the fetus directly through infection and indirectly through the fetal inflammatory response syndrome, which is implicated in preterm birth and neurological injury. Less commonly infection reaches the cavity haematogenously or via invasive procedures.
additionalDifferentials: Maternal fever from another source such as urinary tract infection or respiratory infection
additionalInvestigations: Maternal observations including temperature, heart rate, and continuous fetal heart rate monitoring
Full blood count and inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein
Blood cultures and cultures of genital tract and amniotic fluid where feasible
Amniocentesis for Gram stain, glucose, and culture in selected preterm cases
Placental and membrane histology and culture after delivery to confirm the diagnosis
Screening for group B streptococcus and other genital pathogens
redFlags: Features of maternal sepsis such as high fever, tachycardia, hypotension, or confusion requiring urgent resuscitation and delivery
Non-reassuring or abnormal fetal heart rate patterns indicating fetal compromise
Foul-smelling or purulent amniotic fluid with significant uterine tenderness
Failure to improve despite antibiotics, suggesting the need to expedite delivery
Signs of neonatal sepsis after birth requiring immediate paediatric assessment
reference.prognosis: With prompt antibiotics and timely delivery most mothers recover fully, though the condition carries risks of postpartum infection, haemorrhage from uterine atony, and rarely septic shock. Neonatal outcome depends on gestation and the severity of the fetal inflammatory response; term infants generally do well with treatment, whereas preterm infants exposed to intrauterine infection face higher risks of sepsis and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment.
pitfalls: Attributing maternal fever solely to an epidural and missing intra-amniotic infection
Delaying delivery while attempting to treat the infection conservatively
Underestimating the risk of maternal sepsis and uterine atony after delivery
Failing to alert the neonatal team to the risk of early-onset neonatal sepsis
Overlooking anaerobic and polymicrobial cover in the choice of antibiotics
management: Start prompt broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering ascending genital flora — a penicillin combined with an aminoglycoside and anaerobic cover such as metronidazole or clindamycin
Expedite delivery, since the infection will not resolve while the pregnancy continues, with mode guided by obstetric conditions and foetal status
Give supportive sepsis care with antipyretics, intravenous fluids and oxygen, guided by continuous maternal observation and foetal heart-rate monitoring
Continue antibiotics into the postpartum period, particularly after caesarean, to prevent endometritis
Arrange neonatal team attendance at delivery and paediatric evaluation of the newborn for early-onset sepsis
Monitor for and manage maternal complications including uterine atony with postpartum haemorrhage and wound infection
Escalate to critical care when maternal sepsis progresses to septic shock or organ dysfunction
